claims.text: Optimized spark plasma sintering will produce ultrafine W–Cu interfacial regions.
Optimized spark plasma sintering will improve bonding at W–Cu interfaces.
The SPS-induced interfacial structure will increase the composite's thermal conductivity.
The SPS-processed composite will retain mechanical durability.
The SPS-processed composite will retain irradiation resistance.
Tailoring SPS heating profiles, pressure, and sintering time can refine the W–Cu microstructure.
Tailoring SPS heating profiles, pressure, and sintering time can enhance W–Cu interfacial bonding.
An optimized SPS temperature window can prevent copper melting and excessive grain growth.
Controlled copper-channel dispersion and uniformly bonded W–Cu interfaces reduce thermal boundary resistance.
SPS enables rapid densification with minimal grain coarsening.
The high heating rate and applied pressure used in SPS enhance interfacial bonding.
Enhanced interfacial bonding reduces thermal resistance.
Microstructural refinement during SPS preserves the intrinsic mechanical strength of the constituent materials.
Microstructural refinement during SPS preserves the irradiation stability of the constituent materials.
At equal overall composition, SPS-processed W–Cu will have statistically significantly higher thermal conductivity than conventionally powder-metallurgy-processed W–Cu.
The thermal-conductivity improvement will occur without a measurable decrease in mechanical durability.
The thermal-conductivity improvement will occur without a measurable decrease in irradiation resistance.
Standard powder metallurgy is the current state-of-the-art route for W–Cu composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications.
Scale-up defects or uncontrolled grain coarsening may eliminate the anticipated SPS benefit.
The microstructural benefits of SPS are well recognized.
